**Background:** Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is now the leading cause of chronic liver disease worldwide, affecting more than one-third of adults and tracking the parallel global epidemics of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Its progressive form, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), carries risk of fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, yet until the recent accelerated approvals of resmetirom and semaglutide, no pharmacotherapy was specifically approved for the disease, leaving lifestyle modification as the sole recommended intervention. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and newer dual/triple incretin-based agonists have emerged as candidate disease-modifying therapies, but the evidence base spans mechanistic, trial, and real-world comparative-effectiveness data that vary considerably by drug, disease stage, and outcome definition.

**Methods:** A PRISMA-informed, PubMed-only search (NCBI E-utilities) combining GLP-1RA/incretin and MASLD/MASH terminology identified 100 records; all were retained after deduplication and passed title/abstract screening, yielding 50 included studies spanning 41 journals. No risk-of-bias instrument or dual independent review was applied; single-database coverage is an acknowledged limitation.

**Results:** GLP-1 monotherapy, principally semaglutide, consistently reduces hepatic fat and transaminases and resolves steatohepatitis (pooled odds ratio 3.48 for MASH resolution without fibrosis worsening), but its effect on fibrosis is smaller and statistically fragile, concentrated in F2-F3 disease, with limited signal in compensated cirrhosis. Dual and triple agonists — tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1), and survodutide, mazdutide, pemvidutide, retatrutide, and cotadutide — show larger, more consistent effects on both MASH resolution (pooled relative risk 3.32) and fibrosis improvement (relative risk 1.49), with tirzepatide achieving resolution in up to 62% of patients versus 10% with placebo. Real-world comparisons against SGLT2 inhibitors are mixed, and evidence in compensated cirrhosis and MetALD remains sparse.

**Conclusion:** GLP-1RA monotherapy is well-supported for steatosis-predominant, earlier-stage MASLD/MASH, while dual/triple agonism is the more defensible choice when fibrosis regression is the treatment goal. Durability after discontinuation, efficacy in advanced fibrosis and MetALD, and long-term hepatocellular carcinoma risk-benefit remain unresolved and warrant head-to-head trials and multi-database evidence synthesis.
